home.heroSubtitle: Discover how affordable and clean energy can transform lives, protect our planet, and build a sustainable world for everyone.
home.introText: In 2015, the United Nations adopted 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) to end poverty, protect the planet, and ensure prosperity for all by 2030. Goal 7 focuses on ensuring access to affordable, reliable, sustainable, and modern energy for everyone on Earth.
home.objective1Text: Ensure universal access to affordable electricity and clean cooking solutions, so no family is left in the dark or forced to choose between energy and other basic needs.
home.objective2Text: Build energy systems that work every day, everywhere — resilient grids and infrastructure that can support homes, schools, hospitals, and businesses without interruption.
home.objective3Text: Substantially increase the share of renewable energy, such as solar, wind, and hydropower, in the global energy mix to reduce pollution and fight climate change.

home.windShort: Uses the power of moving air to spin turbines and generate electricity.
home.hydroShort: Harnesses the energy of flowing or falling water to produce electricity.
home.geoShort: Taps into heat stored beneath the Earth's surface for power and heating.
home.actionSubtitle: Big change starts with small, everyday actions. Here's how you can help.
home.action1: Turn off lights and unplug devices when you're not using them.
home.action2: Walk, cycle, or use public transportation instead of a car when possible.
home.action3: Talk to your family about switching to energy-efficient appliances and LED bulbs.
home.action4: Learn about renewable energy and share what you know with friends and classmates.
home.action5: Play Energy Hero to practice making smart energy decisions for a whole city.
home.action6: Use our Energy Calculator to understand your own household's energy use.

about.pageSubtitle: Understanding the United Nations goal for affordable and clean energy.
about.unText: The United Nations (UN) is an international organization founded in 1945, currently made up of 193 member countries. Its mission is to maintain peace, protect human rights, deliver humanitarian aid, and promote sustainable development around the world.
about.sdgText: In September 2015, all UN member states adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which includes 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). SDG 7 is titled 'Affordable and Clean Energy' and calls on the world to ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable, and modern energy for all by 2030.
about.whyAffordableText: Energy is not a luxury — it powers hospitals, schools, refrigeration for food and medicine, clean water systems, and communication. When energy is too expensive, families are forced to make impossible choices, and entire communities are held back from economic opportunity.
about.whyCleanText: Clean energy sources like solar and wind produce electricity without releasing the greenhouse gases and pollutants that come from burning fossil fuels. Choosing clean energy protects the air we breathe, slows climate change, and preserves ecosystems for future generations.
about.fossilText: Coal, oil, and natural gas remain the largest sources of energy worldwide, but burning them releases carbon dioxide and other pollutants. This drives climate change, damages air quality, harms human health, and contributes to habitat destruction from extraction activities like mining and drilling.
about.povertyText: Energy poverty happens when people cannot access or afford reliable modern energy. It forces families to rely on unsafe fuels like kerosene or wood for cooking, limits children's ability to study after dark, and prevents small businesses and clinics from operating effectively.
about.climateText: The energy sector is responsible for a large share of global greenhouse gas emissions. Rising temperatures caused by these emissions lead to more extreme weather, rising sea levels, and disruptions to farming and water supplies — impacting the poorest communities the hardest.
about.efficiencyText: Using less energy to achieve the same result — through better insulation, efficient appliances, and smarter design — is one of the fastest and cheapest ways to cut emissions and lower energy bills at the same time.
about.helpGovText: Governments can invest in clean energy infrastructure, set efficiency standards, and create policies that make renewable energy more accessible and affordable.
about.helpBusinessText: Businesses can invest in renewable technology, improve efficiency in their operations, and develop innovative clean energy solutions.
about.helpIndividualText: Individuals can make everyday choices — like saving energy at home, supporting clean energy policies, and spreading awareness — that add up to meaningful change.
about.timelineSubtitle: A brief history of how clean energy technology has evolved.
about.timeline1Text: French physicist Edmond Becquerel discovers the photovoltaic effect, the scientific basis for solar panels.
about.timeline2Text: James Blyth builds one of the first known wind turbines used to generate electricity, in Scotland.
about.timeline3Text: Bell Labs develops the first practical silicon solar cell capable of powering everyday electrical equipment.
about.timeline4Text: Global oil crises spark renewed interest in renewable energy research and government investment.
about.timeline5Text: Wind and solar technology improve rapidly, and countries begin adopting the first large-scale renewable energy policies.
about.timeline6Text: The United Nations adopts the Sustainable Development Goals, including SDG 7, and the Paris Agreement is signed.
about.timeline7Text: Solar and wind become the cheapest sources of new electricity in most of the world, accelerating the global clean energy transition.
about.targetsSubtitle: The United Nations has set specific targets to measure progress toward SDG 7 by 2030.
about.target1: 7.1 — Ensure universal access to affordable, reliable, and modern energy services.
about.target2: 7.2 — Substantially increase the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix.
about.target3: 7.3 — Double the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency.
about.target4: 7.a — Enhance international cooperation to facilitate access to clean energy research, technology, and investment.
about.target5: 7.b — Expand infrastructure and upgrade technology for supplying modern, sustainable energy services, especially in developing countries.

renewable.pageSubtitle: Explore how different clean energy technologies work, compare their strengths, and discover where they're used around the world.
renewable.compareSubtitle: Click any source below to expand its full details.

solar.name: Solar Energy
solar.how: Photovoltaic (PV) cells convert sunlight directly into electricity, while solar thermal systems use sunlight to heat water or air for buildings and industrial processes.
solar.pros: Abundant and widely available; scalable from a single rooftop to massive solar farms; no emissions during operation; increasingly affordable.
solar.cons: Produces no electricity at night and less on cloudy days; requires significant space for large-scale farms; manufacturing panels has an environmental footprint.
solar.impact: Very low emissions during use, though manufacturing and disposal of panels require careful recycling to minimize environmental impact.
solar.uses: Rooftop panels on homes and businesses, large solar farms, solar water heaters, and portable solar chargers.
solar.fact: Some solar panels can convert sunlight to electricity with efficiencies exceeding 22%, and lab prototypes have gone even higher.

wind.name: Wind Energy
wind.how: Wind turns large turbine blades, which spin a generator inside to produce electricity. Turbines are built on land (onshore) or in bodies of water (offshore).
wind.pros: No fuel costs or emissions during operation; land beneath turbines can still be used for farming; offshore wind can generate very large amounts of power.
wind.cons: Power output depends on wind conditions; can affect local bird and bat populations if not carefully sited; some people are concerned about noise or visual impact.
wind.impact: Minimal emissions during operation, with careful site planning needed to protect wildlife and habitats.
wind.uses: Onshore and offshore wind farms, and small turbines for individual homes or farms.
wind.fact: A single large offshore wind turbine can generate enough electricity to power thousands of homes.

hydro.name: Hydropower
hydro.how: Flowing or falling water spins a turbine connected to a generator. Large dams store water in reservoirs, while 'run-of-river' systems use the natural flow of a river.
hydro.pros: Provides a highly reliable, steady supply of electricity; large dams can also store energy and help control flooding; long lifespan of facilities.
hydro.cons: Large dams can disrupt river ecosystems and displace communities; construction is expensive and site-dependent; can be affected by droughts.
hydro.impact: Low operational emissions, but large dam projects can significantly change local ecosystems and water flow.
hydro.uses: Large-scale national power grids, small run-of-river systems for local communities, and pumped-storage plants for energy storage.
hydro.fact: Hydropower is currently the largest source of renewable electricity generation in the world.

geothermal.name: Geothermal Energy
geothermal.how: Wells are drilled into the Earth to access heat from underground reservoirs of steam or hot water, which drives turbines or heats buildings directly.
geothermal.pros: Provides constant, reliable power regardless of weather or time of day; small physical footprint compared to other sources; long-term low operating costs.
geothermal.cons: Only viable in specific geological locations with accessible heat; high upfront drilling and exploration costs; potential for minor induced seismic activity.
geothermal.impact: Very low emissions, though drilling and fluid management must be handled carefully to avoid contaminating groundwater.
geothermal.uses: Geothermal power plants, direct heating for homes and greenhouses, and geothermal heat pumps for individual buildings.
geothermal.fact: Iceland generates a large share of its electricity and nearly all of its heating from geothermal energy.

biomass.name: Biomass Energy
biomass.how: Organic materials such as wood, agricultural waste, and dedicated energy crops are burned or converted into biogas or biofuels to generate heat and electricity.
biomass.pros: Can use waste materials that would otherwise be discarded; provides a way to manage agricultural and forestry byproducts; can be stored and used on demand.
biomass.cons: Burning biomass releases carbon dioxide and air pollutants; large-scale use can compete with food production for land; sustainability depends heavily on sourcing practices.
biomass.impact: Considered lower-carbon than fossil fuels when sourced sustainably, but poor management can lead to deforestation and air quality issues.
biomass.uses: Biomass power plants, biogas digesters on farms, wood pellet heating systems, and biofuels for transportation.
biomass.fact: Biogas produced from food and animal waste can be used to cook meals, heat homes, or generate electricity.

tidal.name: Tidal Energy
tidal.how: Underwater turbines or barrages capture the kinetic energy of rising and falling ocean tides, converting the predictable motion of water into electricity.
tidal.pros: Extremely predictable, since tides follow well-known astronomical cycles; high energy density due to the weight of water; long equipment lifespan.
tidal.cons: Currently expensive to build and maintain; limited to coastal areas with strong tidal ranges; can affect marine ecosystems near installations.
tidal.impact: Low emissions during operation, but underwater construction can disturb local marine habitats if not carefully managed.
tidal.uses: Coastal tidal barrages, underwater tidal turbine arrays, and emerging small-scale tidal generators for remote coastal communities.
tidal.fact: Because tides are driven by predictable gravitational forces, tidal energy output can be forecast years in advance.

tips.pageSubtitle: Small changes make a big difference. Track your progress as you build sustainable habits.
tips.progressComplete: Amazing! You've completed every tip. You're a true energy hero!

home1.title: Switch to LED bulbs
home1.text: Replace incandescent bulbs with LED lights, which use up to 90% less energy and last much longer.

home2.title: Unplug idle electronics
home2.text: Unplug chargers, TVs, and game consoles when they're not in use to avoid 'phantom' standby power draw.

home3.title: Wash clothes in cold water
home3.text: Most of the energy used by a washing machine goes toward heating water — cold washes save energy and still clean effectively.

home4.title: Improve home insulation
home4.text: Seal drafts around windows and doors and add insulation to reduce the energy needed for heating and cooling.

home5.title: Install a smart thermostat
home5.text: Smart thermostats automatically adjust temperature based on your schedule, avoiding wasted heating or cooling.

home6.title: Air-dry laundry when possible
home6.text: Use a clothesline or drying rack instead of a tumble dryer to save a significant amount of electricity.

school1.title: Turn off classroom lights
school1.text: Switch off lights in empty classrooms, and make use of natural daylight whenever possible.

school2.title: Start an energy-saving club
school2.text: Organize a student group to track school energy use and suggest improvements to staff.

school3.title: Shut down computers overnight
school3.text: Make sure school computers and projectors are fully shut down, not just in sleep mode, at the end of the day.

school4.title: Encourage recycling programs
school4.text: Recycling paper, plastic, and electronics reduces the energy needed to manufacture new materials.

transport1.title: Walk or cycle for short trips
transport1.text: For trips under a couple of kilometers, walking or cycling saves fuel and is great exercise.

transport2.title: Use public transportation
transport2.text: Buses and trains carry many passengers at once, using far less energy per person than individual cars.

transport3.title: Carpool with others
transport3.text: Sharing rides with classmates or coworkers reduces the number of cars on the road and fuel used per trip.

transport4.title: Keep tires properly inflated
transport4.text: Under-inflated tires increase fuel consumption — check tire pressure regularly for better efficiency.

tech1.title: Enable power-saving mode
tech1.text: Turn on power-saving or eco mode on laptops, phones, and monitors to automatically reduce energy use.

tech2.title: Lower screen brightness
tech2.text: Reducing screen brightness on phones, tablets, and computers noticeably extends battery life and saves energy.

tech3.title: Choose energy-efficient appliances
tech3.text: When buying new appliances, look for energy-efficiency labels to choose models that use less electricity.

public1.title: Support solar-powered street lighting
public1.text: Advocate for solar-powered streetlights and public lighting in your community to reduce grid electricity use.

public2.title: Report broken or wasteful lighting
public2.text: Let local authorities know about street lights or public lights that stay on unnecessarily during the day.

public3.title: Use reusable water bottles and bags
public3.text: Producing plastic items requires energy — reusable alternatives reduce that ongoing demand.
